newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli unions in nationwide wildcat strike.
newsitem.headline: Israeli unions in nationwide wildcat strike.

text.p: Israeli unions battling privatisation plans launched a nationwide strike Thursday, grounding summer travelers at Tel Aviv's busy international airport and disrupting rail and postal services.

The Histadrut labour federation said 60,000 workers at state-owned companies or institutions began an open-ended strike in support of employees of Bezeq Israel Telecom in their fight against a further sell-off of the company.
Tel Aviv's Ben-Gurion international airport was particularly hard-hit.
"As of 7:30 a.m. there are no takeoffs. Planes are landing but the only service we are giving them are ramps to unload the passengers," an airport workers' union official told Israel Radio.
Hundreds of passengers who had not known about the strike, announced late Wednesday, packed the departure halls. Airlines advised others to wait at home for word of an end to the stoppage.
"The Histadrut is dragging the economy toward chaos," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's spokesman said in a statement after the strike began.

The labour federation said workers at the Israel Airports Authority, Israel Electric Company, Israeli Military Industries, Israel Aircraft Industries, the Postal Authority, the railroads and other state-owned institutions like El Al Israel Airlines were taking part.

A spokesman for the Israeli Manufacturers' Association said the main damage caused by the strike so far had been "inconvenience." But he warned that a prolonged walkout could cost the economy up to $30 million a day.
Workers' committees leading the strike planned to meet later in the day to discuss whether to continue the stoppage.

"I am going to recommend that we not return to work until the prime minister meets the strike committee or the secretary general of the Histadrut," said Pinhas Inbar, leader of the Airports Authority union.

The stoppage was declared hours after the government issued an order to force hundreds of Bezeq employees to restore essential telephone services disrupted in a week-long strike by workers at the country's main telecommunications provider.

Union leaders at Bezeq called the move "totalitarian" and said a crisis continued over government plans to privatise more of the state-owned company through the $250 million sale of 12.5 percent of its stock to Merrill Lynch.

Union leaders said the Merrill Lynch deal violated government promises to involve Bezeq workers in all aspects of the company's privatisation and called for the sale to be cancelled or to use its revenues to fund early pension programmes.

"(Thursday's) strike is unnecessary and will not affect the government's intention of opening the economy to competition in various fields while protecting workers' rights," Netanyahu's spokesman said.
